questions.question: What are the four gRPC service types and when do you use each?
questions.title: gRPC Service Types — Unary, Server Streaming, Client Streaming, Bidirectional
questions.direct_answer: **gRPC** supports four RPC patterns: **unary** (one request, one response — like a normal function call), **server streaming** (one request, stream of responses — e.g. live updates), **client streaming** (stream of requests, one response — e.g. file upload), and **bidirectional** **streaming** (both sides stream concurrently — e.g. chat or real-time trading feeds). All four are expressed in the `.proto` file using the `stream` keyword.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using unary for everything and polling for updates, when server-streaming is the natural fit. Or writing a bidirectional RPC and never calling `onCompleted()` on the server side, leaving the client's stream open forever.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss cancellation via `Context.current().isCancelled()`, back-pressure in client-streaming, flow control via `CallStreamObserver.setOnReadyHandler`, and when gRPC bidirectional streaming displaces WebSocket for service-to-service real-time.

sections.title: Why Request-Response Isn't Enough — The Problem That Created Streaming RPCs
sections.content:
REST APIs give you one pattern: send a request, wait for a response.
- When your order-tracking UI needs live updates, you poll every 2 seconds — 30 requests per minute per user, most returning "no change." When your IoT gateway receives 10,000 sensor readings per second, each one becomes a separate HTTP request with full headers, TLS handshake overhead, and connection setup.
- The request-response model wasn't designed for continuous data flow.

gRPC solves this with four RPC patterns built on HTTP/2's native stream support.
- The `stream` keyword in your `.proto` file controls the direction of data flow.
- No `stream` keyword means unary — one request, one response.
- Add `stream` to the response and the server can push multiple messages on a single connection.
- Add it to the request and the client streams data to the server.
- Add it to both and you get a full-duplex channel.

The design insight is that all four patterns share the same connection.
- HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over a single TCP connection, so a server-streaming RPC and a unary RPC to the same service share one connection — no additional TCP setup.
- In Java, all four patterns map to the same abstraction: `StreamObserver<T>`.
- Unary and server-streaming methods receive a `StreamObserver<Response>` to push results.
- Client-streaming and bidirectional methods return a `StreamObserver<Request>` that the framework writes incoming messages to.
- The difference is how many times you call `onNext()` and from which side.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`stream` keyword controls direction** — no `stream` = unary, `stream` on response = server streaming, `stream` on request = client streaming, both =.
- **Server streaming replaces polling** — push updates on a single connection instead of clients polling every 2 seconds.
- **`StreamObserver` is the universal abstraction** — unary receives it, streaming returns it.
- **`onError()` and `onCompleted()` are terminal** — calling either one after the other throws `IllegalStateException`.
- **Start with unary, add streaming when justified** — streaming adds lifecycle complexity.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
gRPC gives you four RPC patterns built on HTTP/2 streaming, and the `stream` keyword in the `.proto` file controls which one you get. Each pattern suits different communication needs.

**Unary — the default for most calls:**
- One request, one response — exactly like REST; use it for 90% of service calls including lookups, CRUD operations, and anything request-response
- The simplest lifecycle: call the method, get a result, done; no streaming complexity or cancellation management required

**Server streaming — replacing polling:**
- The client sends one request and the server pushes a stream of responses — live order tracking, log tailing, streaming large query results
- Instead of clients polling every 2 seconds with full request overhead each time, the server pushes updates on a single connection at any rate; the single connection eliminates repeated TLS and HTTP setup costs

**Client streaming:**
- The client sends a sequence of messages and gets one response at the end; natural for chunked file uploads and telemetry batching where you send many small pieces and get a summary confirmation

**Bidirectional streaming:**
- Both sides push independently over a full-duplex channel; chat applications, collaborative editing, and trading feeds with acknowledgments all use this pattern
- The most complex lifecycle: both sides can send or close at any time, so error handling and cancellation require careful design

**Lifecycle safety rules:**
- `onError` and `onCompleted` are both terminal on `StreamObserver` — call either twice and you get `IllegalStateException`
- Always check `Context.current().isCancelled()` in server-streaming loops or you'll keep producing data for disconnected clients

I recommend starting with unary and only adding streaming when polling overhead or per-call latency is a measured problem, not a theoretical one — streaming adds real lifecycle complexity.

sections.title: The Problem with Raw gRPC Setup — And Why the Starter Exists
sections.content:
Setting up a gRPC server without Spring integration means hand-wiring `ServerBuilder`, manually registering services, managing the server lifecycle alongside your application context, and writing your own interceptor plumbing. In a Spring Boot world where `@RestController` auto-registers HTTP endpoints with zero boilerplate, that manual ceremony feels wrong.

The `grpc-spring-boot-starter` from `net.devh` bridges gRPC's runtime with Spring Boot's conventions.
- It scans for beans annotated with `@GrpcService`, registers them with a Netty-based gRPC `Server` instance, and starts that server on a configurable port (default 9090) alongside Spring Boot's HTTP server.
- Your gRPC service implementation is a regular Spring bean — constructor injection, `@Value` properties, `@Transactional` methods all work exactly as you'd expect.

The architectural consequence is that your application now runs **two servers in one process** — the servlet-based HTTP server on port 8080 and the gRPC server on port 9090.
- This means two health checks, two sets of TLS certificates if you're doing mTLS, and two port mappings in your Kubernetes service definition.
- Understanding this dual-server model is the key to avoiding production surprises — from forgotten port mappings to health probes that only check one protocol while the other is unresponsive.

sections.title: Step 1 — Add the Starter and Protobuf Dependencies
sections.content:
The `grpc-spring-boot-starter` bundles `grpc-netty-shaded` as the transport layer, so you don't need to manage Netty dependencies separately. You still need the `protobuf-java` runtime and the `protobuf-maven-plugin` for code generation from your `.proto` files. The starter version tracks Spring Boot's release cadence, so check the compatibility matrix before upgrading.

```xml
<dependencies>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>net.devh</groupId>
    <artifactId>grpc-spring-boot-starter</artifactId>
    <version>2.15.0.RELEASE</version>
  </dependency>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>com.google.protobuf</groupId>
    <artifactId>protobuf-java</artifactId>
    <version>3.25.1</version>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>
```

The production footgun is version compatibility — using Spring Boot 3.2 with a starter built for 2.7 produces cryptic `NoSuchMethodError` exceptions at startup because the starter references Spring APIs that moved between Boot 2 and Boot 3. Always verify the starter version against the project README's compatibility matrix before upgrading Spring Boot.

sections.title: Step 2 — Configure the gRPC Server Port and Properties
sections.content:
By default, the gRPC server binds to port 9090, separate from Spring's HTTP server on 8080. Override this in `application.yml` along with TLS and keepalive settings.

```yaml
grpc:
  server:
    port: 9090                    # dedicated gRPC port
    # security:                   # uncomment for mTLS
    #   certificate-chain: classpath:server.crt
    #   private-key: classpath:server.key

spring:
  application:
    name: order-service
```

Running gRPC on a separate port means your Kubernetes `Service` needs two port definitions, your Ingress or load balancer needs a separate listener for HTTP/2 traffic, and your network policies must allow traffic on both ports. This is the most commonly forgotten step when migrating a REST-only service to dual REST+gRPC — the gRPC port works locally but is unreachable in the cluster because the `Service` manifest only exposes port 8080.

For tests, always set `grpc.server.port: 0` to get a random available port. Hardcoded test ports cause CI failures when two test suites run in parallel and both try to bind 9090.

sections.title: Step 3 — Annotate Your Service and Optionally Wire a Client
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Dual-server model** — the app runs HTTP on port 8080 and gRPC on port 9090 simultaneously.
- **`@GrpcService` = auto-registration** — the starter discovers annotated beans, registers them with the Netty gRPC server, and manages startup/shutdown.
- **`grpc.server.port: 0` in tests** — always use random ports in test properties to avoid CI failures from parallel test suites binding the same port.
- **`@GrpcClient` + YAML addresses** — logical service names map to addresses and TLS negotiation per environment without recompiling.
- **Starter version must match Spring Boot version** — Boot 2.x and 3.x have different Spring APIs.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Setting up a gRPC server in Spring Boot with `grpc-spring-boot-starter` is clean once you understand the dual-server model. Your application runs two servers simultaneously, and both need to be configured correctly.

**The basic setup:**
- Add `net.devh:grpc-spring-boot-starter` dependency, set `grpc.server.port` in `application.yml` — typically 9090 — and annotate your service implementation with `@GrpcService`
- The starter handles Netty server startup, service registration, and lifecycle management alongside the Spring context; your service class is a regular Spring bean with full support for constructor injection, `@Transactional`, and configuration properties
- On the client side, `@GrpcClient` injects a managed stub with a logical service name configured in YAML — addresses can switch from `static://` for dev to `dns://` for production service discovery without recompiling

**The dual-server model — the critical detail:**
- Your application runs HTTP on port 8080 and gRPC on port 9090; that means two health checks, potentially two TLS certificate sets for mTLS, and two port entries in your Kubernetes Service definition
- A common deployment mistake: the K8s manifest exposes only port 8080, so gRPC is unreachable in the cluster with no obvious error — the service starts fine but all gRPC clients get connection refused

**Test configuration:**
- Always set `grpc.server.port: 0` in test properties to use a random port; parallel test suites binding the same port is a frequent CI failure source that's hard to debug

I recommend verifying both ports appear in your Kubernetes Service manifest before the first cluster deployment — and confirming the starter version matches your Spring Boot major version, since Boot 2.x and 3.x have different APIs that cause `NoSuchMethodError` on startup if mismatched.

questions.title: gRPC Interceptors for Auth and Logging

Inside the **interceptor**, access the `Metadata` (headers) for tokens, call `Context` for propagating values, and delegate to the next handler or abort with a `Status.UNAUTHENTICATED` error.

sections.title: Why Cross-Cutting Concerns Can't Live in Service Methods
sections.content:
Imagine adding JWT validation to a gRPC service with 15 RPC methods.
- Without interceptors, every method starts with the same 10 lines — extract the token from metadata, validate it, check roles, abort if invalid.
- When the auth logic changes (new token format, different header name, additional claims check), you update 15 methods.
- Miss one, and that endpoint is unauthenticated in production.

gRPC interceptors solve this the same way servlet filters solve it for HTTP — they wrap every RPC call in a chain that executes before and after the service method.
- A `ServerInterceptor` receives three things: the `ServerCall` (representing the RPC), the `Metadata` (gRPC's equivalent of HTTP headers), and a `ServerCallHandler` (the next interceptor or the service itself).
- The interceptor can inspect headers, reject the call entirely, modify the request, or attach values to the `Context` for downstream use.

The `grpc-spring-boot-starter` makes registration trivial: annotate an interceptor bean with `@GrpcGlobalServerInterceptor` to apply it to every service, or pass specific interceptor classes to `@GrpcService(interceptors = ...)` for per-service scoping.
- The critical difference from Spring's `SecurityContextHolder` is context propagation — gRPC uses explicit `Context` objects instead of `ThreadLocal`, which is essential because streaming RPCs can process messages across different threads.
- Using `ThreadLocal` for auth state in gRPC silently breaks the moment you handle a streaming call.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Interceptors are gRPC's equivalent of servlet filters — they wrap every RPC call so you can centralize logging, authentication, and metrics without touching service methods. Implement `ServerInterceptor`, annotate with `@GrpcGlobalServerInterceptor`, and the starter applies it to every service automatically.

**Logging interceptor:**
- Wrap the `ServerCall` with `ForwardingServerCall` to capture the method name at entry and the status code at exit; override only the methods you need — typically `close()` for response logging — and delegate everything else to avoid breaking flow control or cancellation propagation
- This gives structured request-response logs without modifying any service code

**Auth interceptor:**
- Read the `Authorization` header from gRPC's `Metadata`, validate the JWT, and either close the call with `Status.UNAUTHENTICATED` or attach the principal to a `Context.Key` using `Contexts.interceptCall()`
- Return a no-op `new ServerCall.Listener<>() {}` after calling `call.close()` to prevent the service method from executing on rejected calls — without this, the service still runs after rejection

**The context propagation model — the most important detail:**
- Unlike Spring Security's `SecurityContextHolder` which uses `ThreadLocal`, gRPC's `Context` is explicitly propagated through `Contexts.interceptCall()`
- If you use `ThreadLocal` for auth state, it works fine for unary calls but silently breaks on streaming RPCs where message handlers run on different threads — `Context.Key` propagates correctly across all gRPC execution models

I recommend always using `Context.Key` for anything request-scoped in gRPC, and setting `@Order` on interceptors so auth runs before logging — rejected calls should still appear in access logs.

questions.question: How does gRPC error handling work and what are the key Status codes?
questions.title: gRPC Error Handling with Status Codes
questions.direct_answer: **gRPC** uses a well-defined set of `Status` codes (0–16) instead of HTTP status codes. The server signals errors by calling `responseObserver.onError(StatusRuntimeException)` or by closing the call with a non-OK `Status`. The client receives a `StatusRuntimeException` that it can catch and inspect. You should always map your domain exceptions to meaningful gRPC status codes rather than letting raw Java exceptions propagate.

sections.title: gRPC Has Its Own Error Language — And It's Not HTTP Status Codes
sections.content:
The most common mistake developers make when starting with gRPC is assuming errors work like REST.
- In REST, a 404 means "not found," a 401 means "unauthenticated," and your HTTP client framework parses these automatically. gRPC runs over HTTP/2, but it **does not use HTTP status codes for application errors**.
- Every gRPC call returns HTTP 200 at the transport layer — even failures.
- The actual result lives in the `grpc-status` and `grpc-message` trailers appended to the HTTP/2 response.

gRPC defines 17 canonical status codes (0 through 16), each with precise semantics. `OK`
- means success. `NOT_FOUND`.
- means the requested entity doesn't exist. `INVALID_ARGUMENT`.
- means the client sent bad input. `UNAVAILABLE`.
- means the service is temporarily down — **safe to retry**. `INTERNAL`.
- means an unexpected server error — retrying won't help.

The distinction between `UNAVAILABLE` and `INTERNAL` is critical for production clients.
- Client retry logic branches on the status code — `UNAVAILABLE` triggers exponential backoff retries, while `INTERNAL` surfaces the error to the caller immediately.
- If your server returns `INTERNAL` for a transient database connection timeout instead of `UNAVAILABLE`, clients won't retry and users see errors that would have resolved on the next attempt.

In Java, servers signal errors by calling `responseObserver.onError()` with a `StatusRuntimeException`.
- Clients catch `StatusRuntimeException` and inspect `getStatus().getCode()`.
- The pattern is clean, but the trap is letting raw Java exceptions (NPE, IllegalState) propagate — gRPC wraps them as `UNKNOWN` with the exception message as the description, potentially leaking internal class names and stack traces to the client.

- `StatusRuntimeException.getStatus().getCode()` is the client-side API; always switch on the code enum, not the description string which is human-readable and may change

sections.title: Two Independent Performance Layers That Compound Under Load
sections.content:
Saying "gRPC is faster than REST" without quantifying where the speed comes from is the kind of answer that makes interviewers stop listening. The performance gap exists for two independent reasons, and each one matters at a different scale.

**Layer 1: Serialization.** Protocol Buffers produces binary messages that are 3–10× smaller than equivalent JSON.
- JSON repeats field names in every single object — a list of 1,000 users includes the string `"username"` 1,000 times.
- Protobuf uses field numbers (1 byte each) instead.
- JSON requires runtime parsing — the deserializer scans characters, handles string escaping, infers types dynamically.
- Protobuf's schema is compiled at build time, so deserialization is a direct memory copy with known offsets — no reflection, no type guessing.
- On a service processing 10K messages per second, the CPU savings from avoiding JSON parsing alone can free 20–30% of a core.

**Layer 2: Transport.** gRPC runs over HTTP/2, which multiplexes all RPC calls on a single TCP connection and compresses headers with HPACK.
- REST over HTTP/1.1 requires a new TCP connection per request (or careful connection pooling) and repeats headers verbatim on every call.
- The TLS handshake alone — 1–2 round trips, 50–100ms — disappears when a single persistent HTTP/2 connection handles all calls.
- HPACK header compression is particularly effective for gRPC because most calls to the same service carry identical metadata — after the first request establishes the header table, subsequent requests encode headers in as few as 5 bytes.

These advantages compound in a service mesh.
- When a single user request fans out to 5 downstream services, each saving 5ms of serialization overhead and avoiding per-request connection setup, the aggregate latency reduction reaches 25ms — visible in p99 latency dashboards.
- Teams switching internal hot-path REST calls to gRPC commonly report 60–70% latency reductions.

But context matters.
- For a low-traffic admin API serving 100 requests per minute, the difference is unmeasurable — and REST's ability to debug with curl, test with Postman, and cache with CDNs is worth more than the microseconds you'd save.
- The performance advantage is real but situational — it pays off on high-RPS internal paths and is irrelevant at the edge.

gRPC is faster than REST for internal service calls for two compounding reasons: smaller payloads from Protocol Buffers and connection efficiency from HTTP/2. At scale, these savings compound in ways that REST's simplicity cannot offset.

**Protocol Buffers — the payload advantage:**
- Binary encoding with field numbers instead of repeated key names produces payloads 3–10× smaller than JSON; a list of 1,000 objects avoids repeating field names like "orderId", "customerId", "amount" for every element
- The compiled schema means deserialization is a direct memory copy instead of runtime character scanning, string escaping, and type inference; at 10K messages per second, the CPU savings alone are measurable — roughly 20–30% of a CPU core

- All RPCs share one persistent TCP connection with full multiplexing — multiple in-flight requests without head-of-line blocking
- REST over HTTP/1.1 needs a new connection per request or connection pooling to approach similar efficiency; every new connection repeats the TCP and TLS handshake cost

**Where the advantages compound:**
- In service mesh scenarios with multiple hops, saving 5ms per hop across five services produces 25ms aggregate improvement on a single user request — the deeper the call chain, the larger the total payoff
- Teams have reported cutting internal latency by 60–70% switching high-frequency REST calls to gRPC on measured hot paths

**When gRPC's advantages don't matter:**
- Below roughly 1,000 requests per second, the performance difference is unmeasurable; REST's debuggability with curl, Postman, and browser tooling is a real advantage that gRPC cannot match

I recommend gRPC for east-west traffic on high-RPS internal paths where the performance savings are measurable, and REST at the edge and for low-traffic internal endpoints where debuggability matters more than microseconds.

questions.question: How do deadlines and cancellation work in gRPC, and why are they important?
questions.title: Deadlines and Cancellation in gRPC
questions.direct_answer: A **gRPC** **deadline** is a point in time by which a client expects a response. It is propagated through the entire call chain as part of the context. If the deadline expires, gRPC cancels the call with `Status.DEADLINE_EXCEEDED` on the client and sets the context as cancelled on the server. Every service should respect deadlines — checking `Context.current().isCancelled()` — to avoid doing unnecessary work after the client has already given up.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Deadlines are critical to preventing cascade failures — if a downstream service hangs, a client without a deadline will hold a thread or connection indefinitely, causing resource exhaustion upstream.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Deadlines are critical to preventing cascade failures — if a downstream service hangs, a client without a deadline will hold a thread or connection indefinitely, causing resource exhaustion upstream.

sections.title: The Cascade Failure That Deadlines Exist to Prevent
sections.content:
Picture a common microservice call chain: the API gateway calls the order service, which calls the inventory service, which calls the warehouse database.
- The warehouse database starts running slow — queries that normally take 50ms now take 30 seconds.
- Without deadlines, every layer waits.
- The inventory service holds a thread for 30 seconds.
- The order service holds a thread for 30 seconds.
- The gateway holds a thread for 30 seconds.
- At 100 concurrent requests, that's 300 blocked threads across three services — and none of them can serve new traffic.

This is the **cascade failure** that deadlines prevent.
- A deadline is an **absolute wall-clock timestamp** — not a relative timeout — by which the client expects a response.
- The critical distinction matters: if Service A sets a 500ms deadline and spends 300ms doing local work before calling Service B, Service B inherits only 200ms of remaining budget.
- A naive per-hop timeout of 500ms would give B a fresh window, masking the fact that A's client has already waited 300ms.

gRPC transmits the deadline as the `grpc-timeout` header on every hop, and each downstream service sees the shrinking budget.
- When the deadline expires, two things happen simultaneously: the client receives `Status.DEADLINE_EXCEEDED` and stops waiting, and the server's `Context` is marked as cancelled.
- The server is responsible for checking `Context.current().isCancelled()` — gRPC doesn't kill server threads automatically.
- Without that check, the server finishes processing a request whose result nobody will ever read, wasting CPU, database connections, and queue capacity.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Deadlines are gRPC's primary resilience mechanism and are fundamentally different from per-hop timeouts. A deadline is an absolute wall-clock timestamp, not a relative duration — this distinction drives every cascading behavior in a distributed call chain.

**How deadlines propagate:**
- When you call `stub.withDeadlineAfter(500, MILLISECONDS)`, gRPC converts that to a wall-clock timestamp and propagates it in the `grpc-timeout` header to every downstream hop in the call chain
- Budget subtraction: if Service A sets a 500ms deadline and spends 300ms doing local work before calling Service B, Service B inherits only 200ms — not a fresh 500ms window; this prevents the common pattern where each service gives a fresh timeout and the client's patience is exhausted invisibly

**Server-side cancellation checking:**
- gRPC marks the context as cancelled when the deadline expires but does not interrupt the server thread; without explicit checks, the server continues processing for results nobody will receive
- Always check `Context.current().isCancelled()` inside loops and before expensive operations like database queries; without this, servers waste 30–40% of compute at peak completing work for disconnected clients

**The cascade failure scenario:**
- Without deadlines, a hung downstream service holds threads in every upstream service indefinitely — thread pool exhaustion cascades across the entire call chain
- An RPC without a deadline is a resource leak; every thread waiting for a response that will never come is capacity unavailable for legitimate requests

I recommend establishing a rule that every gRPC stub call gets a deadline — no exceptions — and enforcing it through code review and architecture standards rather than leaving it to individual developer discipline.

questions.question: What is the gRPC health checking protocol and how do you implement it in Spring Boot?
questions.title: gRPC Health Checking Protocol
questions.direct_answer: The **gRPC** Health Checking Protocol is a standard gRPC service defined by Google (`grpc.health.v1.Health`) that exposes a `Check` (**unary**) and `Watch` (**server streaming**) RPC for liveness and readiness probes. Load balancers and orchestrators (Kubernetes, **Envoy**) call `Check` to determine whether a service is ready to accept traffic. The `grpc-spring-boot-starter` auto-configures this service and integrates it with Spring's `HealthIndicator` beans.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Running gRPC in Kubernetes without health checks means the orchestrator cannot detect unhealthy pods.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Interviewers want to see you know both the protocol standard and the Spring Boot integration.

sections.title: Why HTTP Health Endpoints Don't Work for gRPC Services
sections.content:
When Kubernetes needs to check if a REST service is healthy, it sends an HTTP GET to `/actuator/health` and checks for a 200 response. Simple. But a gRPC server speaks HTTP/2 with binary protobuf — an HTTP/1.1 GET request to a gRPC port returns garbage or a connection error. The orchestrator thinks the service is dead when it's perfectly healthy.

Before Kubernetes 1.24, teams worked around this by running a sidecar HTTP health endpoint or using `grpc_health_probe` as a custom exec command.
- Both approaches were fragile — the sidecar could be healthy while the gRPC server was crashed, and the exec probe had a cold-start cost on every check.
- Kubernetes 1.24 added **native gRPC probes** that speak the protocol directly, eliminating these workarounds.

The gRPC Health Checking Protocol is defined in `grpc.health.v1.Health` — a standard `.proto` file that all gRPC implementations understand. It exposes two RPCs: `Check` returns the current health status as one of `SERVING`, `NOT_SERVING`, `UNKNOWN`, or `SERVICE_UNKNOWN`. `Watch` is a server-streaming RPC that pushes status changes in real time — useful for load balancers like Envoy that want to react to health transitions without constant polling.

The protocol supports **per-service granularity** through the `service` field in the request.
- An empty string checks overall health, but you can report different statuses for different services on the same server — the `UserService` is healthy while the `PaymentService` is degraded because its downstream database is slow.
- This lets the load balancer route around a specific degraded service without marking the entire pod as unhealthy.

sections.title: Step 1 — Auto-Configuration in Spring Boot and Actuator Integration
sections.content:
The `grpc-spring-boot-starter` registers the `grpc.health.v1.Health` service automatically — no code needed. It bridges Spring Actuator's `HealthIndicator` beans to gRPC health status: when Spring reports DOWN (database unreachable, Redis timeout), the gRPC health service flips to `NOT_SERVING`, and Kubernetes stops routing traffic to that pod.

```yaml
grpc:
  server:
    port: 9090
    health-service-enabled: true    # default is true

management:
  endpoint:
    health:
      probes:
        enabled: true               # enable liveness/readiness separation
```

You can verify the health service is responding using `grpcurl` from the command line — this is the gRPC equivalent of curling an HTTP health endpoint.

```bash
# Check overall health
grpcurl -plaintext localhost:9090 grpc.health.v1.Health/Check
# Response: { "status": "SERVING" }

# Check a specific service
grpcurl -plaintext -d '{"service": "OrderService"}' \
  localhost:9090 grpc.health.v1.Health/Check
```

If your application has custom health requirements beyond Spring Actuator's defaults — for example, verifying that a Kafka consumer is caught up or that a cache is warm — implement a `HealthIndicator` bean. The starter picks it up automatically and includes it in the gRPC health response.

sections.title: Step 2 — Configure Kubernetes Native gRPC Probes
sections.content:
Kubernetes 1.24+ supports gRPC probes directly in the pod spec. The kubelet calls the `Check` RPC on the configured port, and the pod transitions to unready if the response is anything other than `SERVING`.

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: order-service
    image: myregistry/order-service:2.1
    ports:
    - containerPort: 9090
    livenessProbe:
      grpc:
        port: 9090
      initialDelaySeconds: 10
      periodSeconds: 10
    readinessProbe:
      grpc:
        port: 9090
        service: ""              # empty = overall health
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 5
```

The critical production rule is **separating liveness from readiness**. Liveness checks whether the process itself is healthy — a stuck thread, a deadlock, an out-of-memory condition. If liveness fails, Kubernetes restarts the pod. Readiness checks whether the pod can accept traffic — database connected, caches warm, downstream dependencies available. If readiness fails, Kubernetes removes the pod from the Service's endpoint list but doesn't restart it.

Confusing the two causes cascading restarts. If a database goes slow and you report that as a liveness failure, Kubernetes restarts every pod in the deployment. The restarted pods reconnect to the same slow database, fail liveness again, and restart in a loop — an outage that amplifies the original problem. Use readiness for dependency failures (stop traffic, let the dependency recover) and liveness only for process-level problems (the JVM is stuck).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **HTTP health checks don't work on gRPC ports** — an HTTP/1.1 GET to a gRPC server returns garbage.
- **`grpc-spring-boot-starter` auto-registers the health service** — bridges Spring `HealthIndicator` beans to gRPC status.
- **Per-service granularity via the `service` field** — an empty string checks overall health.
- **Liveness ≠ readiness** — liveness failure restarts the pod; readiness failure stops traffic without restart.
- **`Watch` RPC for reactive health monitoring** — server-streaming RPC pushes status transitions to Envoy in real time without constant polling overhead.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The gRPC Health Checking Protocol is a standard service every production gRPC deployment needs from day one. HTTP health endpoints don't work on gRPC ports — an HTTP GET to a gRPC port returns garbage because gRPC speaks HTTP/2 with binary protobuf framing.

**The protocol:**
- The standard service at `grpc.health.v1.Health` exposes two RPCs: `Check` returns the current status — `SERVING` or `NOT_SERVING` — and `Watch` is a server-streaming RPC that pushes status changes in real time to load balancers without constant polling
- The `service` field provides per-service granularity — an empty string checks overall health; a specific service name lets load balancers route around degraded services without marking the entire pod unhealthy

**Spring Boot integration:**
- With `grpc-spring-boot-starter`, the health service is auto-configured and wired to Spring Actuator's health indicators; if a database connection fails, Actuator reports DOWN, the gRPC health flips to `NOT_SERVING`, and Kubernetes removes the pod from traffic rotation
- Kubernetes 1.24+ supports native gRPC probes — configure `grpc.port: 9090` in `livenessProbe` and `readinessProbe` directly; no workarounds needed

**The liveness vs readiness distinction — the most important rule:**
- Liveness failure triggers a pod restart; readiness failure stops traffic without restarting
- A slow database should fail readiness (drain traffic) but not liveness (don't restart the pod); confusing the two causes cascading restarts that amplify an existing outage — every restart triggers a reconnect storm that makes a struggling database worse

I recommend wiring health checks to your database and external dependency indicators from day one, and always keeping liveness and readiness as separate probes with different thresholds.

questions.direct_answer: Test **gRPC** services at three levels: unit tests that mock `StreamObserver` and call the service implementation directly; integration tests that use `grpc-spring-boot-starter`'s `@SpringBootTest` with an in-process server; and end-to-end tests that start a real server and call it via a generated blocking stub. sections.title: Why MockMvc Can't Test gRPC — And What Replaces It
sections.content:
In a REST world, `MockMvc` lets you test controllers without starting a real HTTP server — it simulates the entire request pipeline in-memory.
- When you migrate to gRPC, that tool disappears. `MockMvc` speaks HTTP/1.1 with JSON bodies; gRPC speaks HTTP/2 with binary protobuf and a completely different header and trailer model.
- Your first instinct — "I'll just curl the gRPC port in a test" — creates slow, flaky tests that depend on port availability and network behavior.

gRPC's testing toolchain replaces `MockMvc` with two mechanisms. For unit tests, the service implementation is a plain Java class — instantiate it directly, pass a mocked `StreamObserver`, and assert on what gets sent. No server, no network, no Spring context. Tests run in single-digit milliseconds.

For integration tests, `InProcessServerBuilder` and `InProcessChannelBuilder` from the `grpc-testing` library start a real gRPC server and client inside the same JVM with no TCP socket. The server processes requests through the full protobuf serialization path, interceptor chain, and `StreamObserver` lifecycle — catching bugs that unit tests miss (metadata propagation, interceptor ordering, serialization edge cases) — while remaining fast and deterministic.

The testing pyramid still applies: many fast unit tests for business logic, fewer integration tests for wiring and interceptor behavior, and a small number of end-to-end tests that exercise the full Spring Boot context including `@GrpcService` auto-configuration and `@GrpcClient` injection.

sections.content:
- **`MockMvc` doesn't work for gRPC** — it speaks HTTP/1.1+JSON; gRPC requires direct service invocation (unit) or in-process server/channel (integration).
- **Mocked `StreamObserver` unit tests run in <10ms** — verify `onNext`, `onCompleted`, and `onError` contract without any server or Spring context.
- **`InProcessServerBuilder` exercises the full protobuf path** — serialization, interceptor chain, and status code mapping without TCP sockets.
- **`grpc.server.port=-1` disables TCP in Spring tests** — combined with `in-process-name`, routes all traffic through in-process transport.
- **Error path tests are non-negotiable** — assert specific `Status.Code` values on the thrown `StatusRuntimeException`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The key difference from REST testing is that `MockMvc` doesn't work for gRPC — it speaks HTTP/1.1 with JSON, and gRPC needs HTTP/2 with protobuf. Test at three levels with the right tools for each.

**Unit tests — fastest and simplest:**
- Instantiate the service directly as a plain Java object, pass a mocked `StreamObserver`, and assert that `onNext` was called with the expected response and `onCompleted` was called; no Spring, no server, no network
- Use `ArgumentCaptor` to inspect the response object's fields; these run in under 10 milliseconds and give fast feedback on business logic

**Integration tests — full gRPC pipeline without TCP:**
- Use `InProcessServerBuilder` from the `grpc-testing` library to start a real gRPC server inside the JVM with no TCP socket; this exercises full protobuf serialization and the interceptor chain while staying fast and deterministic
- `GrpcCleanupRule` handles channel and server shutdown so you don't leak threads or channels across test runs

**Spring Boot tests — full context, no port binding:**
- Use `@SpringBootTest` with `grpc.server.port=-1` and `in-process-name` to route everything through in-process transport; the full Spring context boots — `@GrpcService` discovery, interceptors, health service — but without binding a real port, eliminating CI port conflicts

**Error path tests — non-negotiable:**
- Assert that the stub throws `StatusRuntimeException` with the correct status code for every error scenario — `NOT_FOUND` for missing entities, `INVALID_ARGUMENT` for bad input, `UNAUTHENTICATED` for missing tokens
- Untested error paths are the first thing that breaks when real clients hit edge cases; the test `assertThrows(StatusRuntimeException.class, () -> stub.callMethod(...)).getStatus().getCode()` pattern is straightforward

I recommend unit tests for every service method, integration tests for every interceptor behavior, and at least one error path test per distinct `Status.Code` the service can return.
